notes: Tall shelves (main-left, main-right, leadership) are the standing collection. Stool, O’Reilly, and the stoic/investor display are currently on the desk. Main-right bottom row and main-left top row are the same physical shelf photographed from two angles — catalogued once under main-right.

books.title: The Daily Stoic
books.author: Ryan Holiday & Stephen Hanselman
books.summary: A page-a-day companion drawn from Marcus Aurelius, Seneca, and Epictetus. Holiday turns stoic practice into a working discipline: control what you can, meet fortune without drama, and keep a journal honest enough to change you.
books.whyItFits: Jonas talks about judgment and giving people the keys back. A daily stoic page is the same muscle he asks leaders to use with AI — pause, ask better questions, don’t outsource the hard part.

books.title: Meditations
books.author: Marcus Aurelius
books.summary: The private notes of a Roman emperor writing to himself. Not a system so much as a repeated return to duty, mortality, and composure under pressure.
books.whyItFits: A consulting lead who teaches executives sits closer to Marcus than to a manifesto: do the work in front of you, stay useful, don’t get drunk on the tool.

books.title: The Daily Drucker
books.author: Peter F. Drucker
books.summary: A year of Drucker in short takes: effectiveness, contribution, and the job of a manager as someone who makes other people’s work possible.
books.whyItFits: Team Lead at BDO Digital. Drucker is the daily version of ‘start with the outcome, then pick the technology.’

books.title: The Daily Laws
books.author: Robert Greene
books.summary: Greene’s corpus — power, seduction, mastery, human nature — cut into a page a day. Useful as a map of other people’s games, dangerous if you start playing them for sport.
books.whyItFits: Sits with 48 Laws on the tall shelf. The desk copy is the one you actually open before a hard meeting.

books.title: The Art of Doing Science and Engineering
books.author: Richard W. Hamming
books.summary: Hamming’s end-of-career lectures on how to do work that matters: style in science, the courage to look stupid, and learning to learn. Stripe Press gave it a second life.
books.whyItFits: The night-school years in Python were Hamming’s assignment whether Jonas had the book yet or not. Now it sits on the desk.

books.title: Poor Charlie's Almanack
books.author: Peter D. Kaufman (ed.), Charlie Munger
books.summary: Munger’s talks on multidisciplinary mental models, inversion, and the lollapalooza of getting incentives right. A latticework against one-tool thinking.
books.whyItFits: Jonas’s method for AI work is value, feasibility, and risk — inversion in consulting clothes. Munger is the same instinct with different jokes.

books.title: The Scaling Era: An Oral History of AI, 2019–2025
books.author: Dwarkesh Patel with Gavin Leech
books.summary: Stripe Press oral history of the scaling years: labs, capital, and the people who bet that more compute would keep working. Recent enough to still feel like a briefing.
books.whyItFits: The lightbulb around generative AI came with a responsibility hangover. This is the recap of the years he has been teaching through.

books.title: The Origins of Efficiency
books.author: Brian Potter
books.summary: Potter on how industries actually get cheaper and faster — construction, manufacturing, the unglamorous history of productivity. Stripe Press again.
books.whyItFits: Feasibility is one of the three screens. Origins of Efficiency is the long view of why some ideas ship and others stay slides.

books.title: The Intelligent Investor
books.author: Benjamin Graham
books.summary: Graham’s classic on value investing and Mr. Market. Margin of safety, temperament over tips, and the difference between investing and speculation.
books.whyItFits: A decade in alternative investments at Citco, then quant research on the side — this is the foundation text for not confusing a model’s confidence with a thesis.

books.title: Quantum Physics Made Me Do It
books.author: Jérémie Harris
books.summary: A physicist-turned-AI-person on what quantum weirdness does — and does not — license in the rest of life. Witty, library-stickered, currently on the stool.
books.whyItFits: The stool pile is the curiosity stack. Harris is the bridge from popular physics to the AI questions already on the desk.

books.title: How Data Happened
books.author: Chris Wiggins & Matthew L. Jones
books.summary: A history from the age of reason to the age of algorithms: how counting people became a political technology, not just a scientific one.
books.whyItFits: Data strategy that starts with the business objective is a historical claim. Wiggins and Jones are the origin story.

books.title: Deep Thinking
books.author: Garry Kasparov
books.summary: Kasparov on Deep Blue, human–machine teams, and why losing to a computer did not end the argument about judgment. Where machine intelligence ends and creativity begins, from someone who had to find out in public.
books.whyItFits: Jonas teaches executives not to outsource the hard part. Kasparov lost to the machine and still insists the human stays in the loop.

books.title: Quantum Computing For Dummies
books.author: whurley & Floyd Earl Smith
books.summary: A yellow-spine field guide to qubits, gates, and why the hype cycle is running ahead of the hardware. Library copy, 2024 sticker still on it.
books.whyItFits: The tinkerer’s version of keeping up: read the dummy book before you nod along in a client meeting.

books.title: AI Engineering
books.author: Chip Huyen
books.summary: Huyen on building applications with foundation models: evaluation, RAG, orchestration, and the unglamorous work that makes a demo into a system. Owl on the cover; the spine is the copy in play.
books.whyItFits: This is the craft book under ‘Building AI Projects That Deliver.’ Foundation models are the tool; Huyen is the how.

books.title: Financial Theory with Python
books.author: Yves Hilpisch
books.summary: Hilpisch teaching the theory — cash flows, uncertainty, optimization — in Python instead of a chalkboard. Thin spine, heavy math.
books.whyItFits: Accounting degree plus night-school Python. This is the book that makes those two halves talk to each other.

books.title: Python for Algorithmic Trading
books.author: Yves Hilpisch
books.summary: From data ingestion to backtests to deployment, written for people who will actually run a strategy. O’Reilly’s trading-desk Python book.
books.whyItFits: The GitHub line is quantitative finance. Hilpisch is the working manual, not a think-piece.

books.title: Python for Finance
books.author: Yves Hilpisch
books.summary: The red one: pandas, NumPy, and derivatives analytics for people who came from Excel and refuse to go back. Hilpisch’s flagship.
books.whyItFits: Jonas lists Pandas on his profile for a reason. This is the O’Reilly that belongs next to the Citco years.

books.title: The Aeneid
books.author: Virgil (tr. Allen Mandelbaum)
books.summary: Rome’s origin poem: duty over desire, a city founded by a man who keeps leaving. Mandelbaum’s translation stacked on the leadership bay.
books.whyItFits: A leadership shelf that starts with Aeneas is making a point about obligation, not charisma.

books.title: The Odyssey
books.author: Homer (tr. Richmond Lattimore)
books.summary: The long way home. Lattimore’s line-by-line Homer, lying on top of the business books like a reminder that cunning and endurance are older than OKRs.
books.whyItFits: Consulting is mostly getting people home through other people’s storms. Odysseus would recognize the calendar.

books.title: Principles
books.author: Ray Dalio
books.summary: Dalio’s operating system: believability-weighted decisions, pain plus reflection, and the idea that a firm can be an idea meritocracy if you write the rules down.
books.whyItFits: Value, feasibility, risk — Jonas already runs a short principles list. Dalio is the long form.

books.title: Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order
books.author: Ray Dalio
books.summary: Empires, debt cycles, and reserve currencies plotted as if history were a trading account. Sweeping, arguable, and very Dalio.
books.whyItFits: A decade in fund services makes you allergic to ‘this time is different.’ Dalio is the chart version of that allergy.

books.title: Zero to One
books.author: Peter Thiel with Blake Masters
books.summary: Thiel’s brief against incrementalism: competition is for losers, monopoly is the point, and the future is not evenly distributed.
books.whyItFits: Growth Pod advising wants founders to pick a real secret. Thiel is the sharpest — and most arguable — version of that talk.

books.title: Never Split the Difference
books.author: Chris Voss
books.summary: An FBI hostage negotiator on tactical empathy, calibrated questions, and why ‘fair’ is often a trap. Penguin spine, well-worn.
books.whyItFits: Client rooms are negotiations whether anyone admits it. Voss is how you listen without caving.

books.title: King of Capital
books.author: David Carey & John E. Morris
books.summary: The rise of Blackstone: private equity as a machine for buying, fixing, and charging fees. A biography of a firm, not a hero.
books.whyItFits: Alternatives were the day job for a decade. Carey and Morris are the view from the other side of the NAV.

books.title: What Makes Great Leaders Great
books.author: Gene A. Klann
books.summary: Fifty-two leaders, fifty-two short lessons — a field manual more than a theory. Practical to a fault, which is the point.
books.whyItFits: Jonas’s father was a teacher and a coach. Klann is the leadership shelf’s drill-card version of that house.

books.title: The Goal
books.author: Eliyahu M. Goldratt
books.summary: A business novel that smuggles in the Theory of Constraints: find the bottleneck, subordinate everything else, repeat. Subtitle still on the spine — a process of ongoing improvement.
books.whyItFits: AI projects stall on the real constraint, which is rarely the model. Goldratt is the diagnostic.

books.title: Legal, Tax & Accounting Strategies for the Canadian Real Estate Investor
books.author: George Dube & various
books.summary: The Canadian practitioner’s book: entities, GST, recapture, and the ways a deal looks different after the CRA has a look.
books.whyItFits: BComm Accounting, Halifax. This is the local craft book, not a Tony Robbins spine.

books.title: Financial Intelligence
books.author: Karen Berman & Joe Knight
books.summary: Finance for people who run things: what the numbers mean, how they get massaged, and which questions to ask when the slide is too clean.
books.whyItFits: Jonas came up through accounting. This is the translation layer he wishes every client team already had.

books.title: Dark Money
books.author: Jane Mayer
books.summary: Mayer on the Koch network and the long project of moving American politics with other people’s money, quietly.
books.whyItFits: Incentives again. If you work around capital, you should know how it buys the weather.

books.title: The Undoing Project
books.author: Michael Lewis
books.summary: Lewis on Kahneman and Tversky: the friendship that invented behavioral economics, and the undoing of the rational-agent fairy tale.
books.whyItFits: Concordia teaching keeps returning to professional judgment. This is the origin story of why fluent answers mislead.

books.title: The Fifth Risk
books.author: Michael Lewis
books.summary: What happens when a government is handed to people who do not want to know how it works. Lewis on competence as a public good.
books.whyItFits: ‘If it damages trust, it is not a good idea.’ Lewis wrote the civic version of that sentence.

books.title: Flash Boys
books.author: Michael Lewis
books.summary: Speed, fiber, and the fight over whether public markets are still public. A story about infrastructure posing as strategy.
books.whyItFits: HFT-adjacent curiosity and a tinkerer’s respect for pipes. The market is a system, not a vibe.

books.title: Boomerang
books.author: Michael Lewis
books.summary: Lewis’s post-crash travelogue: Iceland, Ireland, Greece, Germany, California — the same cheap money, different local humiliations.
books.whyItFits: Fund-services years make this less exotic than it looks. Cheap leverage travels.

books.title: Liar's Poker
books.author: Michael Lewis
books.summary: Salomon Brothers as a human comedy of bonds, egos, and the 1980s. The book that made market culture visible to everyone else.
books.whyItFits: Financial services from the inside, written with enough bite to keep a consultant from romanticizing the sell side.

books.title: What the Dog Saw
books.author: Malcolm Gladwell
books.summary: Gladwell’s magazine pieces: ketchup, hair dye, the talent myth, and the rest of the New Yorker bag. Shorter, looser, still sticky.
books.whyItFits: The leadership bay has the full Gladwell run. This is the one that shows how he thinks in public.

books.title: David and Goliath
books.author: Malcolm Gladwell
books.summary: Underdogs, disadvantages that become advantages, and the costs of being the giant. Gladwell at his most arguable.
books.whyItFits: Nontraditional path — accounting, funds, then Data & AI — is the point, not a detour. Gladwell named the pattern.

books.title: Blink
books.author: Malcolm Gladwell
books.summary: Thin-slicing: when snap judgment is expertise, and when it is prejudice in a hurry.
books.whyItFits: Professional judgment is the Concordia theme. Blink is the warning label.

books.title: The Tipping Point
books.author: Malcolm Gladwell
books.summary: How little things become epidemics — connectors, mavens, stickiness. The book that made ‘going viral’ a business plan.
books.whyItFits: AI adoption inside a firm is a contagion problem. Gladwell’s first book is still the map.

books.title: Outliers
books.author: Malcolm Gladwell
books.summary: The 10,000-hour argument, plus the quieter point that luck, culture, and birth month do more than talent wants to admit.
books.whyItFits: Two to three years of nights learning Python while doing the day job. Outliers is honest about the hours and the accident.

books.title: Talking to Strangers
books.author: Malcolm Gladwell
books.summary: Why we misread people we do not know, and the institutions that pretend otherwise. Gladwell after the easy optimism.
books.whyItFits: Client work is talking to strangers for a living. This is the cautionary edition.

books.title: This Is a Call: The Life and Times of Dave Grohl
books.author: Paul Brannigan
books.summary: Grohl from Springfield to Nirvana to Foo Fighters — work rate as a personality. The odd one out on the leadership shelf, and not really.
books.whyItFits: The tinkerer’s ethic in a different industry. Show up, play the gig, start another band.

books.title: Discipline Equals Freedom
books.author: Jocko Willink
books.summary: Willink’s field manual: wake up early, do the thing, stop negotiating with yourself. Less story, more orders.
books.whyItFits: Nights of Python after a full Citco day only work if someone protects the hours. This is that defense, shouted.

books.title: Extreme Ownership
books.author: Jocko Willink & Leif Babin
books.summary: Former Navy SEALs on the simple, severe idea that if the team failed, you own it. Decentralized command and no bad teams, only bad leaders.
books.whyItFits: Responsibility and accountability are the words Jonas uses for AI. This is that ethic without the lab coat.

books.title: The Dichotomy of Leadership
books.author: Jocko Willink & Leif Babin
books.summary: The sequel: extreme ownership still holds, but so does the opposite — lead and follow, aggressive and careful, all at once.
books.whyItFits: Teaching executives is a dichotomy problem. Push the room without breaking it.

books.title: Leadership Strategy and Tactics
books.author: Jocko Willink
books.summary: Willink’s Q&A book: how to take over a team, how to disagree with your boss, how not to be a tyrant about it.
books.whyItFits: Team Lead is a tactics job. This is the field pocket, not the memoir.

books.title: Quench Your Own Thirst
books.author: Jim Koch
books.summary: The Samuel Adams founder on building a beer company without waiting for permission — stubbornness as a business plan.
books.whyItFits: Self-taught, still shipping. Koch is the founder version of that sentence, with better hops.

books.title: Hedge Fund Due Diligence
books.author: Jason A. Scharfman
books.summary: Operational DD for people who allocate: fraud, service providers, and the questions that belong before the lock-up.
books.whyItFits: Citco Fund Services is the other side of this book. Scharfman is how allocators looked at shops like the ones Jonas supported.

books.title: Young Money
books.author: Kevin Roose
books.summary: Roose embedded with first-year analysts on the Street. The hours, the hazing, the slow leak of a personality.
books.whyItFits: A useful reminder of the culture Jonas did not stay in. The work can be the same numbers with a different soul.

books.title: The Tao of Warren Buffett
books.author: Mary Buffett & David Clark
books.summary: Short Buffettisms, unpacked. A pocket book more than a treatise, sitting between Young Money and Sorkin.
books.whyItFits: Sits near Graham on this bay. The desk has the original; this is the aphorism deck.

books.title: Too Big to Fail
books.author: Andrew Ross Sorkin
books.summary: The 2008 weekend, reconstructed almost minute by minute. Banks, Treasury, and the moment the system asked to be saved.
books.whyItFits: Risk management is in the original skill list. Sorkin is the worked example at system scale.

books.title: Winning
books.author: Jack Welch with Suzy Welch
books.summary: Welch’s GE catechism: differentiation, candor, and the brutality of being number one or two. Famous, dated, still on the shelf.
books.whyItFits: A consulting lead has to know the gospel clients were raised on, even when he does not preach it.

books.title: Good to Great
books.author: Jim Collins
books.summary: Collins’s study of companies that made the leap — Level 5 leadership, the Hedgehog Concept, and a culture of discipline. Famous, argued-over, still useful as a prompt.
books.whyItFits: The Growth Pod advising work is hedgehog-shaped: AI strategy for operators who already know their business.

books.title: The Intelligent Investor
books.author: Benjamin Graham
books.summary: Second copy, on the leadership bay rather than the desk. Same Graham, different job: the standing reference next to Lynch and Malkiel.
books.whyItFits: The desk copy is in rotation. This one stays with One Up On Wall Street so the argument can continue without walking rooms.

books.title: One Up On Wall Street
books.author: Peter Lynch
books.summary: Lynch’s amateur-advantage book: invest in what you see, do the homework, and don’t get bored out of a compounder.
books.whyItFits: Quant research is more honest when it has to live next to Lynch’s grocery-store epiphanies.

books.title: A Random Walk Down Wall Street
books.author: Burton G. Malkiel
books.summary: The efficient-market argument in public: index, diversify, ignore the noise. A counterweight to every clever backtest.
books.whyItFits: Not every edge is an edge. Malkiel is the seatbelt on the Hilpisch pile.

books.title: Big Data Baseball
books.author: Travis Sawchik
books.summary: The 2013 Pirates and the second wave of sabermetrics — shifts, pitching plans, and a small-market team using data as a weapon.
books.whyItFits: Moneyball’s cousin, closer to the dashboard era. Proof that a model only matters if the clubhouse uses it.

books.title: Successful Change
books.author: Susan Cole
books.summary: A practitioner’s change book — green spine, Canadian enough to belong on this bay with the tax and TFSA titles.
books.whyItFits: AI transformation is a change-management job pretending to be a technology job. Cole names the actual work.

books.title: Trading: Technical Analysis Masterclass
books.author: Rolf Schlotmann & Moritz Czubatinski
books.summary: Charts, structure, and the mechanics of reading a tape without mysticism. A how-to, not a memoir.
books.whyItFits: The tinkerer’s trading notebooks need a craft book. This is the one that does not promise a Lamborghini.

books.title: Business Adventures
books.author: John Brooks
books.summary: Brooks’s New Yorker company stories — Xerox, the crash, the Edsel. Buffett and Gates both kept copies. Still the best business writing on the shelf.
books.whyItFits: Narrative as due diligence. Brooks is how you learn a company without a deck.

books.title: A Thousand Barrels a Second
books.author: Peter Tertzakian
books.summary: Tertzakian on the energy chokepoint: demand, geopolitics, and the speed at which the world drinks oil.
books.whyItFits: Macro on a Canadian shelf. Energy is a Halifax conversation whether you are in funds or in data.

books.title: Rise of the Robots
books.author: Martin Ford
books.summary: Ford on automation and labor: what happens to jobs when the robots are not a metaphor. The cover still has the robot.
books.whyItFits: The faculty-lounge version of ‘what happens to the people.’ Jonas’s people-first line has to survive this book.

books.title: How to Win Friends and Influence People
books.author: Dale Carnegie
books.summary: The original soft-skills book: remember names, don’t argue, make the other person glad they met you. Older than everyone in the room and still in print.
books.whyItFits: Teaching executives is Carnegie whether you cite him or not. The spine is honest about that.

books.title: AI Needs You
books.author: Verity Harding
books.summary: Harding — DeepMind policy alum — on the political choices inside AI, using the histories of space, IVF, and the internet as warnings.
books.whyItFits: Responsible AI delivery is on the skills list. Harding is the policy book that belongs next to the O’Reilly stack.

books.title: Primal Leadership
books.author: Daniel Goleman, Richard Boyatzis & Annie McKee
books.summary: Emotional intelligence as a management system: resonance, climate, and the idea that the leader’s nervous system is the team’s weather.
books.whyItFits: ‘We need to bring our people along with us.’ Goleman is the human half of the AI transformation speech.

books.title: The Power of Habit
books.author: Charles Duhigg
books.summary: Cue, routine, reward — and how organizations get stuck in loops they no longer notice. Duhigg’s sticky frame.
books.whyItFits: Two to three years of nights learning Python. Duhigg is how a career actually turns, one loop at a time.

books.title: The Almanack of Naval Ravikant
books.author: Eric Jorgenson
books.summary: Naval’s tweets and talks rearranged into a book: specific knowledge, leverage, and not selling your time forever.
books.whyItFits: Self-taught, still shipping, allergic to theatre. Naval is the internet’s version of that posture.

books.title: The Psychology of Money
books.author: Morgan Housel
books.summary: Housel argues that doing well with money is less about spreadsheets than behavior — humility, patience, and room for error.
books.whyItFits: Bridges the Citco years and the tinkerer’s quant notebooks: returns are a lagging indicator of temperament.

books.title: Limited Liability Companies
books.author: Canadian practitioner guide
books.summary: A practitioner spine on LLCs / Canadian private-company form — the entity book that sits with the TFSA title.
books.whyItFits: Accounting-trained. The structure of the deal is the deal.

books.title: Tax-Free Savings Accounts
books.author: Gordon Pape
books.summary: Pape’s Canadian TFSA guide — contribution room, beneficiary designations, and the quiet power of a tax-free compounding bucket.
books.whyItFits: Halifax, not Manhattan. The personal-finance shelf is allowed to be local.

books.title: Flash Boys
books.author: Michael Lewis
books.summary: Second copy on the same bay, lower shelf — the trading-microstructure story kept with Lefèvre and the banking texts.
books.whyItFits: When a book earns two spots, it is because the argument did not finish the first time.

books.title: Reminiscences of a Stock Operator
books.author: Edwin Lefèvre
books.summary: The Livermore novel: tape reading, blow-ups, and the idea that the market is a teacher who charges tuition.
books.whyItFits: Every quant notebook needs this ghost. Livermore is what happens when temperament fails.

books.title: Toward Prosperity
books.author: Mills & Campbell
books.summary: Canadian policy spine — Mills and Campbell on growth, institutions, and the unglamorous work of getting richer as a country.
books.whyItFits: The civic cousin of the TFSA book. Prosperity is a system, not a mood.

books.title: Investment Banking
books.author: Samuel L. Hayes & Philip Hubbard
books.summary: A thick institutional text: how banks actually make money on deals, and the culture that grows around that money.
books.whyItFits: Fund services sits next to banking, not inside it. Hayes and Hubbard are the map of the neighboring building.

books.title: Dark Genius of Wall Street
books.author: Edward J. Renehan Jr.
books.summary: Jay Gould without the cartoon villainy — or anyway, with the cartoon filled in. Railroad marauder as American type.
books.whyItFits: A reminder from the alternatives world: elegant structures plus other people’s money is still a story about people.

books.title: Banker to the Poor
books.author: Muhammad Yunus
books.summary: Yunus on Grameen Bank and microcredit: the argument that poor people are creditworthy if you bother to build the institution.
books.whyItFits: Jonas’s north star question — who do you serve, what community impact — is the moral of this book in plainer clothes.

books.title: Diary of a Hedge Fund Manager
books.author: Keith McCullough
books.summary: A practitioner diary from the top, to the bottom, and back again — the 2008 vintage from inside a fund.
books.whyItFits: NAV, lock-ups, and the feeling of a month that will not end. Citco people know this weather.

books.title: Endure
books.author: Cameron Hanes
books.summary: Hanes on bowhunting and suffering on purpose. Grit as a training plan, not a personality test.
books.whyItFits: Sits under Willink. The leadership bay’s physical-culture shelf is not a metaphor if you actually do the miles.

books.title: The Will to Win
books.author: Unknown (spine title only)
books.summary: A dark spine whose title is the whole argument: the will to win. Author not readable in the photo.
books.whyItFits: Keeps company with Endure and Extreme Ownership. The bay is not shy about this theme.

books.title: The Lean Six Sigma Pocket Toolbook
books.author: Michael L. George, John Maxey, David Rowlands & Mark Price
books.summary: DMAIC in your jacket: tools, templates, and the unromantic work of taking variation out of a process.
books.whyItFits: Consulting that ships has to survive a process audit. This is the pocket version of that survival.

books.title: Rich Dad Poor Dad
books.author: Robert T. Kiyosaki
books.summary: The popular parable of assets vs. liabilities. Easy to mock, still the book a lot of rooms actually read first.
books.whyItFits: On a shelf with Graham and Lynch it looks like the on-ramp. That is a legitimate job for a book.

books.title: Net Worth
books.author: Unknown (spine title only)
books.summary: A thick blue spine titled Net Worth — personal-finance / Canadian wealth, author not readable in the photo.
books.whyItFits: Sits with the TFSA guide. The household balance sheet is allowed on this bay.

books.title: Canadian Securities Course
books.author: CSI Global Education
books.summary: The CSI textbook: Canadian markets, regulation, and the license a lot of this country’s industry still runs through.
books.whyItFits: Accounting plus alternatives. This is the domestic exam book, not a New York memoir.

books.title: Team of Teams
books.author: Gen. Stanley McChrystal
books.summary: McChrystal on tearing up org charts so information moves at the speed of the fight. Special operations as a management case.
books.whyItFits: IT and the business not sharing a language is a team-of-teams failure. McChrystal named the structure.

books.title: How the Mighty Fall
books.author: Jim Collins
books.summary: Collins’s sequel in a darker key: hubris, undisciplined expansion, denial of risk, grasping for salvation.
books.whyItFits: Risk is one of the three screens. Collins catalogued what it looks like when a firm skips that screen.

books.title: Project Management
books.author: Unknown (spine title only)
books.summary: A textbook spine that simply says Project Management — the delivery manual on a bay otherwise full of memoirs.
books.whyItFits: AI initiatives connected to a three-to-five-year plan still have a Gantt chart. This is that honesty.

books.title: Reinvention
books.author: Unknown (spine title only)
books.summary: A dark spine titled Reinvention. Author not readable; the word is the whole pitch.
books.whyItFits: Accounting to Data & AI is a reinvention. The shelf is allowed to say it plainly.

books.title: The Nvidia Way
books.author: Tae Kim
books.summary: Kim on Huang, CUDA, and the culture that rode the AI wave with more than luck. A company biography written while the story is still expensive.
books.whyItFits: The scaling era on the desk needs the chip-company book on the bay. Hardware is the quiet half of every LLM slide.

books.title: The Corporate Board
books.author: Unknown (spine title only)
books.summary: A thick governance text. How boards actually work, or fail to — title readable, author not.
books.whyItFits: Consulting that talks to leadership eventually talks to a board. This is the civics book for that room.

books.title: Learn to Earn
books.author: Peter Lynch & John Rothchild
books.summary: Lynch’s intro to markets for people who did not grow up speaking ticker symbols. The on-ramp next to Start with Why.
books.whyItFits: Teaching is in the family. Lynch wrote the beginner book and put it on a grown-up shelf.

books.title: Start with Why
books.author: Simon Sinek
books.summary: The golden-circle book: why, how, what — in that order. Easy to parody, still the sentence a lot of rooms need.
books.whyItFits: ‘When you start with the problem, you eventually land on the right application.’ Sinek is the poster version of Jonas’s quote.

books.title: The Black Swan
books.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
books.summary: On the outsized role of rare events and the narrative fallacy that makes them look inevitable afterward. Fragility as a design problem.
books.whyItFits: ‘It looked good on a spreadsheet’ is not a defense. Taleb is the seatbelt.

books.title: The Man Who Solved the Market
books.author: Gregory Zuckerman
books.summary: Jim Simons, Renaissance, and the quant revolution told as a human story: mathematicians, secrecy, and a track record that still looks like a glitch.
books.whyItFits: The Hilpisch pile on the desk wants this ghost story. Medallion is what ‘edge’ looks like when it is real — and closed.

books.title: Exceptional Selling
books.author: Jeff Thull
books.summary: Thull on complex B2B sales: diagnosis before pitch, and the discipline of not rescuing a buyer from their own confusion.
books.whyItFits: Consulting is selling whether you like the word. Thull is the anti-theatre version.

books.title: Fierce Conversations
books.author: Susan Scott
books.summary: Scott on the conversation as the relationship. Interrogate reality, be present, and stop having the meeting after the meeting.
books.whyItFits: Teaching executives and mentoring founders requires the same move: tell the truth without performing toughness.

books.title: When McKinsey Comes to Town
books.author: Walt Bogdanich & Michael Forsythe
books.summary: The Times investigation as a book: opioids, governments, and the firm that will optimize anything you pay it to.
books.whyItFits: A consultant’s shelf should include the indictment. If it damages trust, it is not a good idea — including when the slide is beautiful.

books.title: Steal the Show
books.author: Michael Port
books.summary: Port on performance as a professional skill: talks, pitches, and the ethics of being worth watching.
books.whyItFits: Concordia stages and client rooms are shows. Port is the craft book for not wasting the room.

books.title: Nine Minutes on Monday
books.author: James Robbins
books.summary: A short weekly leadership checklist: meaning, connection, competence. Nine minutes, every Monday, no speech required.
books.whyItFits: Team Lead is a cadence job. Robbins is the smallest possible operating system.

books.title: Cold Hard Truth on Men, Women & Money
books.author: Kevin O'Leary
books.summary: O’Leary’s Canadian money sermon: spend less than you make, don’t romance a balance sheet, Dragon energy included.
books.whyItFits: Local celebrity finance, on a bay that also holds Graham. The contrast is the point.

books.title: Born to Play
books.author: Dustin Pedroia with Bob Hohler
books.summary: Pedroia’s undersized-second-baseman memoir: chip, work, World Series. Sports as a leadership pamphlet that can actually hit.
books.whyItFits: The bay already has Big Data Baseball. Pedroia is the clubhouse half of that argument.

books.title: The SAS Survival Handbook
books.author: John 'Lofty' Wiseman
books.summary: The classic field manual: fire, water, first aid, and how not to die in the woods. Wrapped, practical, unembarrassed.
books.whyItFits: Halifax and Nova Scotia trails are not a metaphor. Sometimes a handbook is a handbook.

books.title: Deutsch für Alle
books.author: Werner Haas & Gustave B. Mathieu
books.summary: A college German textbook: becoming college German, a comprehensive approach. Wiley spine, old-school drills.
books.whyItFits: The collection is allowed to include the language you actually studied. Not every spine has to be a thesis.

books.title: Hiking Trails of Nova Scotia
books.author: Michael Haynes
books.summary: The Goose Lane / local guide: where to walk in this province, how far, how wet. A Halifax book on a Halifax shelf.
books.whyItFits: The bio is geographically specific on purpose. Haynes is the outdoor half of that sentence.

books.title: Steve Jobs
books.author: Walter Isaacson
books.summary: Isaacson’s authorized brick: adoption, calligraphy, the reality distortion field, and the cost of being that person.
books.whyItFits: Product taste as a management style. Useful, and a warning.

books.title: The Product Manager's Handbook
books.author: Linda Gorchels
books.summary: Positioning, roadmaps, and the unglamorous job of being the person who owns the thing. A handbook, as advertised.
books.whyItFits: AI-enabled workflows still need a product owner. Gorchels is the pre-hype version of that job.

books.title: Tools of Titans
books.author: Tim Ferriss
books.summary: Ferriss’s giant interview scrapbook: routines, supplements, and the occasional idea that survives the hype.
books.whyItFits: The tinkerer’s bathroom book. Next to Jobs it looks like a method; next to Clean Code it looks like a dare.

books.title: Macroeconomics
books.author: Christopher Ragan & Richard Lipsey
books.summary: The Canadian undergrad brick — twelfth Canadian edition on the spine. IS-LM, banks, and the closed-economy diagrams you never fully forget.
books.whyItFits: Sobey School of Business. This is the textbook that still justifies opening the footnotes.

books.title: VBA and Macros: Microsoft Excel 2013
books.author: Bill Jelen & Tracy Syrstad
books.summary: Que’s Excel power-user book: loops, UserForms, and the macros that ran finance before pandas did.
books.whyItFits: A decade in fund services is an Excel decade. Jelen is the craft book from that era, honestly kept.

books.title: Accounting Principles and Practice
books.author: R. G. H. Smails & C. E. Walker
books.summary: A battered Canadian accounting text — Smails and Walker, cloth, the real old thing. Principles, then practice, in that order.
books.whyItFits: BComm Accounting. This is the ancestor, not a decoration.

books.title: The Elements of Quantitative Investing
books.author: Giuseppe A. Paleologo
books.summary: Paleologo’s Wiley text on the building blocks: signals, risk, and the difference between a backtest and a business.
books.whyItFits: Quant research on the side needs a grown-up manual. This is the one that does not flatter you.

books.title: Advanced Portfolio Management
books.author: Giuseppe A. Paleologo
books.summary: A risk-manager’s book: P&L explain, factor models, and how a book actually blows up. Eleventh-edition seriousness in a thin spine.
books.whyItFits: Citco valuation work plus tinkerer’s notebooks. Paleologo is the adult supervision.

books.title: Getting Started in Options
books.author: Michael C. Thomsett
books.summary: Wiley’s on-ramp to calls, puts, and why premium is never free. The blue one.
books.whyItFits: Options literacy without the YouTube. A serious amateur’s book, kept with the futures sibling.

books.title: Getting Started in Futures
books.author: Todd Lofton
books.summary: Lofton’s Wiley intro to commodities and the leverage that makes them famous. Black spine, no nonsense.
books.whyItFits: Futures are how a lot of ‘quant’ actually starts. Lofton is the honest first book.

books.title: The Pragmatic Programmer
books.author: Andrew Hunt & David Thomas
books.summary: Craft habits for people who write software for a living: orthogonality, tracer bullets, and not setting the building on fire with cleverness.
books.whyItFits: Self-taught, still shipping. The Pragmatic Programmer is the missing CS department.

books.title: Clean Code
books.author: Robert C. Martin
books.summary: Uncle Bob’s rules of thumb: names, functions, the boy-scout rule. Preachy, useful, still the book people mean.
books.whyItFits: A self-taught developer who now ships Next.js needs the book that makes the first decade of code less accidental.

books.title: Building Applications with AI Agents
books.author: Michael Albada
books.summary: O’Reilly on agentic systems: tools, memory, evaluation, and the gap between a loop and a product. Albada on the spine.
books.whyItFits: ElectroLearn and the Ollama tutor are agent projects. This is the shelf copy of that curiosity.

books.title: Fundamentals of Data Engineering
books.author: Joe Reis & Matt Housley
books.summary: The modern data stack without the vendor haze: ingestion, storage, transformation, serving. O’Reilly’s grown-up DE book.
books.whyItFits: Data platforms only work if the pipes are real. Reis and Housley are the book you hand a room that wants a model before it wants a schema.

books.title: Colossus
books.author: D. F. Jones
books.summary: The 1966 SF novel about a defense computer that decides it knows better — two matching dark spines at the end of the tech row.
books.whyItFits: Next to the AI-agents O’Reilly, Colossus is not subtle. The collection has a sense of humor about control problems.

books.title: The Fall of Berlin 1945
books.author: Antony Beevor
books.summary: Beevor’s endgame: the last weeks of the Reich, assembled from archives and the people who were there. Penguin orange.
books.whyItFits: The history bay starts with a city falling. Scale, logistics, and what ‘victory’ costs.

books.title: World War II: Blitzkrieg, Siege, Counterattack, Victory
books.author: Time-Life Books
books.summary: A four-volume illustrated set in a slipcase: Blitzkrieg, Siege, Counterattack, Victory. Campaign history as a boxed object.
books.whyItFits: Kept with Beevor. The collection likes its war history in both narrative and encyclopedia form.

books.title: The Wealth of Nations
books.author: Adam Smith
books.summary: The division of labour, the invisible hand, and the moral philosophy hiding inside a book people cite without opening.
books.whyItFits: Accounting plus markets. Smith is the origin text, not a decoration, even if the pin factory is a cliché.

books.title: Letters from a Stoic
books.author: Seneca
books.summary: Moral letters on time, friendship, wealth, and how to live without being owned by either luxury or fear. Seneca writes like a counselor who has seen power up close.
books.whyItFits: The desk has Holiday and Marcus. This is the older letter-writer, filed with Nietzsche instead of the dailies.

books.title: Beyond Good and Evil
books.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
books.summary: Nietzsche against the philosophers’ prejudices: a prelude to a philosophy of the future, as advertised, and still a live grenade.
books.whyItFits: A stoic display on the desk does not get to pretend Nietzsche is not in the building.

books.title: Fire and Ice
books.author: R. J. McMaster
books.summary: A worn red-spine novel — R. J. McMaster — keeping company with the philosophy row. Local enough, battered enough to have been read.
books.whyItFits: Not every spine on a serious bay is a textbook. The collection includes the paperbacks that actually got finished.

books.title: Theory of Games and Economic Behavior
books.author: John von Neumann & Oskar Morgenstern
books.summary: The book that made game theory a field: expected utility, minimax, and the idea that strategy is mathematics.
books.whyItFits: Quant research is downstream of this brick. Von Neumann is already on the science row; here he is in economist clothes.

books.title: Nicomachean Ethics
books.author: Aristotle
books.summary: Virtue as a mean, friendship as a civic technology, and the question of what a human life is for. Oxford spine.
books.whyItFits: Judgment, responsibility, the good. Aristotle is the long version of the Concordia lecture.

books.title: Wisdom Takes Work
books.author: Ryan Holiday
books.summary: Holiday’s later stoic title — wisdom as a practice, not a vibe. Sits between Aristotle and Herodotus like a contemporary footnote.
books.whyItFits: The desk has The Daily Stoic. This is the same author arguing that the page-a-day is not the whole job.

books.title: The History
books.author: Herodotus (tr. David Grene)
books.summary: The first historian: inquiry, gossip, and the wars between Greece and Persia. Grene’s Chicago translation.
books.whyItFits: Inquiry is the job. Herodotus named it and then refused to stay in his lane — a useful professional model.

books.title: The Republic
books.author: Plato
books.summary: Justice, the cave, the philosopher-king, and the argument that a city is a soul at scale. Still the book you argue with.
books.whyItFits: Teaching leaders is a Republic problem: who should decide, and on what knowledge.

books.title: The Divine Comedy
books.author: Dante Alighieri
books.summary: Hell, Purgatory, Paradise — a moral cosmology in terza rima, kept with Plato and Twain like it belongs in the same argument.
books.whyItFits: A leadership-and-markets house still needs a map of sin. Dante is not subtle about the destination.

books.title: The Innocents Abroad
books.author: Mark Twain
books.summary: Twain’s pilgrimage send-up: Americans in the Old World, unimpressed and hilarious. Reader’s Digest binding on this copy.
books.whyItFits: Skepticism as style. Twain is the American cousin of the ‘does this actually make sense’ question.

books.title: The Call of the Wild / White Fang / The Sea-Wolf
books.author: Jack London
books.summary: A Greenwich House omnibus: the dog books and The Sea-Wolf, plus forty short stories. Survival as a literary genre.
books.whyItFits: Sits under the SAS handbook. The collection likes its wilderness in both fiction and fieldcraft.

books.title: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Other Stories
books.author: Mark Twain
books.summary: Octopus Treasury of World Masterpieces: Sawyer, Finn, The Prince and the Pauper, Pudd’nhead Wilson, the Connecticut Yankee.
books.whyItFits: The humor that keeps a serious shelf from becoming a shrine. Twain gets two spines and earns both.

books.title: The Complete Tales of Mystery and Imagination
books.author: Edgar Allan Poe
books.summary: Poe’s tales plus Pym and the poems, in the matching Octopus binding. The raven, the heart, the house coming down.
books.whyItFits: A systems person is allowed a gothic. Detection and doom are both information problems.

books.title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.summary: Holmes omnibus: Adventures, Memoirs, Return, Study in Scarlet, Sign of Four, Hound of the Baskervilles. The method, bound in green.
books.whyItFits: Observation before theory. Holmes is the detective version of ‘start with the problem.’

books.title: Tess / The Mayor of Casterbridge / Far from the Madding Crowd
books.author: Thomas Hardy
books.summary: Peerage Books Hardy: Wessex, fate, and people crushed by the plot they were born into.
books.whyItFits: Not everything is a process you can improve. Hardy is the counter-Goldratt.

books.title: The Time Machine / The Invisible Man / The War of the Worlds
books.author: H. G. Wells
books.summary: Peerage Wells: Time Machine, Invisible Man, Island of Dr Moreau, First Men in the Moon, War of the Worlds, Food of the Gods.
books.whyItFits: SF as a way to think about technology before you deploy it. Wells got there early and did not flinch.

books.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
books.author: Daniel Kahneman
books.summary: Kahneman splits cognition into fast intuition and slow analysis, then shows how biases sneak into expert judgment.
books.whyItFits: Required reading if your job is to keep humans from blindly trusting a fluent answer. The Concordia lecture in book form.

books.title: The Art of War
books.author: Sun Tzu (tr. John Minford)
books.summary: The Minford translation: terrain, spies, and the idea that the best battle is the one you do not have to fight.
books.whyItFits: Strategy as information. Minford’s Art of War sits with Greene because the collection treats power as a craft.

books.title: The 33 Strategies of War
books.author: Robert Greene
books.summary: Greene’s war book: grand strategy, defensive war, dirty war. The dark spine with WAR in red, next to 48 Laws.
books.whyItFits: The desk has The Daily Laws. This is the same author in campaign mode.

books.title: The 48 Laws of Power
books.author: Robert Greene
books.summary: The modern courtier’s handbook. Amoral on purpose; useful as a field guide to other people’s games.
books.whyItFits: Client politics are not a rounding error. Greene is the unsentimental map.

books.title: The Book of Five Rings
books.author: Miyamoto Musashi
books.summary: Musashi’s school of the two-sword style, written as a book about seeing. Earth, water, fire, wind, void.
books.whyItFits: Craft, repetition, no theatrics. The swordsman version of Hamming.

books.title: The Prince
books.author: Niccolò Machiavelli
books.summary: How a new prince keeps a state. Honesty about power so blunt that his name became an insult.
books.whyItFits: Filed with Greene and Musashi. The collection does not pretend leadership is only stewardship.

books.title: Nexus
books.author: Yuval Noah Harari
books.summary: Harari on information networks — from the stone age to AI — and the political danger of a system that cannot admit error.
books.whyItFits: The community-impact question sits on a longer timeline than a sprint. Nexus is the Harari that is about this decade.

books.title: Homo Deus
books.author: Yuval Noah Harari
books.summary: After Sapiens: what happens when famine, plague, and war recede and the new projects are immortality, happiness, and divinity.
books.whyItFits: The wide shot for a Data & AI lead. Harari’s future is the scary version of the pitch deck.

books.title: Sapiens
books.author: Yuval Noah Harari
books.summary: A wide history of how shared fictions — money, law, gods, limited companies — let strangers cooperate. Sweeping, arguable, hard to unread.
books.whyItFits: The long shelf. Shared fictions include both markets and models.

books.title: 21 Lessons for the 21st Century
books.author: Yuval Noah Harari
books.summary: Harari’s present-tense book: work, liberty, religion, and how to live when the stories are glitching.
books.whyItFits: The faculty-lounge companion to Nexus. Twenty-one lessons, one of which is ‘you will not keep up by reading faster.’

books.title: Weapons of Math Destruction
books.author: Cathy O'Neil
books.summary: How scoring systems punish the poor, launder bias, and call it objective. A necessary cold shower for anyone selling models to institutions.
books.whyItFits: If it damages trust, it is not a good idea. O’Neil is the worked example.

books.title: A Life Decoded
books.author: J. Craig Venter
books.summary: Venter’s genome memoir: racing the public project, sailing, and the claim that life is information you can read.
books.whyItFits: Biology as a data problem. Sits with Sagan and Dawkins because the collection treats science as a single argument.

books.title: The Dragons of Eden
books.author: Carl Sagan
books.summary: Sagan on the evolution of human intelligence: brains, sleep, and the dragons we still carry. Pulitzer-winning popular science.
books.whyItFits: The wonder half of the science row. Sagan is how you stay curious without getting sloppy.

books.title: The Demon-Haunted World
books.author: Carl Sagan
books.summary: Science as a candle in the dark: baloney-detection, UFOs, and the civic case for not believing whatever feels true.
books.whyItFits: Professional judgment is a baloney-detection kit. Sagan wrote the user’s manual.

books.title: Subliminal
books.author: Leonard Mlodinow
books.summary: How the unconscious mind rules behavior — the subtitle is on the spine. Mlodinow’s tour of the hidden layer.
books.whyItFits: Kahneman’s neighbor. The fast system has a physicist’s explanation too.

books.title: Deep Learning
books.author: Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio & Aaron Courville
books.summary: The MIT Press brick: feedforward nets, regularization, convnets, and the math you actually need. Dark spine, no marketing.
books.whyItFits: Hands-on curiosity is on the GitHub. This is the theory book that makes the tutorials less magical.

books.title: The Computer and the Brain
books.author: John von Neumann
books.summary: Von Neumann’s last lectures: how a computer is and is not like a nervous system. Foreword by Ray Kurzweil on this copy.
books.whyItFits: The original analogical sin of AI, written by one of the people who built the machine. Required humility.

books.title: On the Origin of Species
books.author: Charles Darwin
books.summary: The argument that changed the furniture of the world. Variation, selection, descent — still clearer than most of its descendants.
books.whyItFits: A science row without Darwin is a pose. This copy is the Signet that actually gets pulled.

books.title: Deep Simplicity
books.author: John Gribbin
books.summary: Gribbin on chaos and complexity: how simple rules make the weather, the market, and the rest of the mess.
books.whyItFits: Risk, models, and the illusion of control. Gribbin is the physicist’s Black Swan.

books.title: The Principia
books.author: Isaac Newton (tr. I. Bernard Cohen & Anne Whitman)
books.summary: The mathematical principles of natural philosophy, in the modern English of Cohen and Whitman. Gravity, in the original.
books.whyItFits: The collection’s claim that first principles still matter. Newton is not there for the vibe.

books.title: The Tides of Mind
books.author: David Gelernter
books.summary: Gelernter on thinking as a tide — focus at noon, association at dusk — and what that means for machines that never sleep.
books.whyItFits: An AI shelf that includes a critic of computational arrogance. Gelernter is that critic with a memory-theory.

books.title: A Brief History of Time
books.author: Stephen Hawking
books.summary: Black holes, the Big Bang, and the famous last line about the mind of God. The popular physics book everyone owns for a reason.
books.whyItFits: Wonder, again. The science row is allowed to be for civilians.

books.title: The River of Time
books.author: Igor Novikov
books.summary: Novikov on time, cosmology, and the physicist’s version of ‘can you go back.’ Cambridge spine.
books.whyItFits: Keeps Hawking company. The collection likes its time books in pairs.

books.title: Adaptation and Natural Selection
books.author: George C. Williams
books.summary: Williams against group selection: adaptation is for genes, and most of the stories we tell about ‘for the good of the species’ are wrong.
books.whyItFits: A necessary cold shower next to the pop-science. Williams is how you keep Darwin from turning into a TED talk.

books.title: Maths in Bite-Sized Chunks
books.author: Chris Waring
books.summary: A Michael O’Mara-style explainer: the useful bits of math, in public language, with diagrams.
books.whyItFits: Teaching non-specialists is the Concordia job. Bite-sized is a legitimate design goal.

books.title: Science in Bite-Sized Chunks
books.author: Knowledge series
books.summary: The matching yellow explainer: science in public, no lab coat required.
books.whyItFits: Sits with the math sibling. The collection includes the books you can hand across a table.

books.title: Incognito
books.author: David Eagleman
books.summary: Eagleman on the brain as a team of rivals: how much of you is not available to you, and what that does to the idea of a self.
books.whyItFits: Judgment, again. If most of cognition is offstage, ‘trust the fluent answer’ is malpractice.

books.title: The Selfish Gene
books.author: Richard Dawkins
books.summary: Genes as the unit of selection, organisms as vehicles, and a metaphor that rewired a generation of readers.
books.whyItFits: Williams in popular clothes. The science row ends on the book that made the argument travel.

books.title: Data Mining: Practical Machine Learning Tools and Techniques
books.author: Ian H. Witten, Eibe Frank & Mark A. Hall
books.summary: The WEKA book, third edition: classifiers, clustering, and the unglamorous evaluation that keeps a model honest. Morgan Kaufmann.
books.whyItFits: Before foundation models, this was how a data person learned to not lie with a confusion matrix.

books.title: Cryptonomicon
books.author: Neal Stephenson
books.summary: Codebreaking, data havens, and the joke that the war for information did not end in 1945. Stephenson at full length.
books.whyItFits: A data professional’s novel. Crypto, pipes, and the long game — filed with the war books on purpose.

books.title: Inside the Third Reich
books.author: Albert Speer
books.summary: Speer on architecture, armaments, and the excuse of being ‘just the technician.’ Read as a primary document, not a confession.
books.whyItFits: The technician’s alibi is the whole problem with ‘I just built the model.’ Speer is the warning that will not stay in 1945.

books.title: A Brief History of the Birth of the Nazis
books.author: Nigel Jones
books.summary: Jones on the Freikorps-to-Hitler years: how a movement is born in the wreckage of a war. Short, pointed, red spine.
books.whyItFits: Kept with Speer. The collection does not treat this history as background music.

books.title: The Lost Symbol
books.author: Dan Brown
books.summary: Brown’s Washington puzzle-box: Masons, a tank, and the usual 24-hour footrace. Airport literature, owned honestly.
books.whyItFits: The thriller row starts here. Not every book has to be a briefing.

books.title: American Assassin
books.author: Vince Flynn
books.summary: Mitch Rapp’s origin: a grieving recruit turned into a weapon. Flynn’s first-in-chronology, kept with the rest of the spy paperbacks.
books.whyItFits: The standing thriller row is a Halifax weekend habit. Rapp is the house blend.

books.title: The Black Box
books.author: Michael Connelly
books.summary: Bosch, a 1992 riot-week murder, and a bullet that waited twenty years. Connelly’s procedural patience.
books.whyItFits: Detection as a job. Connelly is the modern Holmes on this wall.

books.title: The Narrows
books.author: Michael Connelly
books.summary: Bosch vs. the Poet, the Los Angeles River, and the case that will not stay closed.
books.whyItFits: Second Connelly on the row. The collection buys authors in runs.

books.title: Black Hawk Down
books.author: Mark Bowden
books.summary: Mogadishu, hour by hour. Journalism that reads like a novel and is worse because it happened.
books.whyItFits: Team of Teams on the leadership bay; this is the night the org chart met the street.

books.title: V2
books.author: Robert Harris
books.summary: Harris on the rocket war: a German engineer, a British WAAF, and the mathematics of a weapon that arrives before its sound.
books.whyItFits: Engineering plus war plus calculation. Harris sits at the intersection this house actually lives in.

books.title: The Autobiography of Malcolm X
books.author: Malcolm X with Alex Haley
books.summary: The conversion narrative that is also a political education: Detroit Red, the Nation, Mecca, the split.
books.whyItFits: A shelf that talks about community impact without this book is bluffing. Haley and Malcolm are the correction.

books.title: The Godfather's Revenge
books.author: Mark Winegardner
books.summary: Winegardner’s authorized sequel: the Corleones in the 1960s, still in the family business. Based on characters created by Mario Puzo.
books.whyItFits: Crime as a management literature. The Godfather books are org-design with worse HR.

books.title: Lord of the Flies
books.author: William Golding
books.summary: Boys on an island, the conch, the fire, the hunt. The shortest argument against ‘we’ll figure out the culture later.’
books.whyItFits: Teams without a Circle of Safety. Golding is the fable version of that failure.

books.title: War and Peace
books.author: Leo Tolstoy
books.summary: The Modern Library Giant: Napoleon, Natasha, and the claim that history is not made by the people who think they are making it.
books.whyItFits: Scale. Tolstoy is what a three-to-five-year plan looks like when it collides with a real war.

books.title: The Return of the King
books.author: J. R. R. Tolkien
books.summary: The end of the third volume: the black gate, the coronation, and the Scouring. Methuen paperback, actually read.
books.whyItFits: The collection owns two-thirds of the trilogy in matching paperbacks. Fellowship is next to it; Two Towers is the gap.

books.title: The Fellowship of the Ring
books.author: J. R. R. Tolkien
books.summary: The walk out of the Shire. Matching Methuen to Return of the King.
books.whyItFits: A long project with a fellowship. Tolkien is allowed to be comfort on a war-and-thriller shelf.

books.title: Shackleton's Way
books.author: Margot Morrell & Stephanie Capparell
books.summary: Ernest Shackleton as a management case: hire for character, keep the crew alive, sell the mission when the ice wins.
books.whyItFits: Endurance is already on the leadership bay as a title. This is the Antarctic original.

books.title: To Kill a Mockingbird
books.author: Harper Lee
books.summary: Scout, Atticus, and the trial in Maycomb. The American civics novel, Penguin binding on this copy.
books.whyItFits: Judgment, again, in a courtroom. Lee is the moral education the professional books assume you already had.

books.title: A Short History of Nearly Everything
books.author: Bill Bryson
books.summary: Bryson’s tour of the universe in plain English: how we found out, and how often we were almost wrong. Blue-grey spine beside Mockingbird.
books.whyItFits: The civilian science book on the fiction row. Bryson is how you keep the wonder without the textbook.

books.title: German-English Science Dictionary
books.author: Louis De Vries
books.summary: McGraw-Hill, battered, De Vries. The dictionary you need if the paper is in German and the experiment will not wait.
books.whyItFits: Keeps company with Deutsch für Alle on the other bay. The language study was not a phase.

books.title: The Wings of Night
books.author: Thomas H. Raddall
books.summary: Raddall, Doubleday, a Nova Scotia novelist on a Nova Scotia shelf. Night, weather, and the Atlantic as a character.
books.whyItFits: Halifax is not a branding detail. Raddall is the local literature the hiking guide implies.

books.title: David Copperfield
books.author: Charles Dickens
books.summary: Dickens’s favorite child: the warehouse, the aunt, the villains, the long becoming. Cloth, worn, actually owned.
books.whyItFits: A Victorian education in luck, work, and other people’s houses. The collection’s longest novel after Tolstoy.

books.title: The Road Ahead
books.author: Bill Gates
books.summary: Gates in 1995 on the internet that was coming. Viking, landscape on the spine, the future as a Microsoft memo.
books.whyItFits: A period piece kept on purpose. The last time a tech memoir tried to name the next twenty years.

books.title: American Sniper
books.author: Chris Kyle with Scott McEwen & Jim DeFelice
books.summary: Kyle’s memoir of Ramadi, the rifle, and the cost of being very good at a terrible job. Harper spine.
books.whyItFits: Filed with No Hero and Call Sign Chaos. The collection’s war shelf is not only the 1945 books.

books.title: Lost Light
books.author: Michael Connelly
books.summary: Bosch off the job, a four-million-dollar heist, and a case from 1995 that will not stay lost. Third Connelly on the wall.
books.whyItFits: The thriller row continues below the Tolkien. Connelly is the house detective.

books.title: Deadline
books.author: John Sandford
books.summary: A Virgil Flowers novel — the rural Minnesota cop who looks like a surfer and is not. Berkley spine.
books.whyItFits: Procedural as comfort food. Sandford keeps company with Child and Flynn.

books.title: The 6:20 Man
books.author: David Baldacci
books.summary: A commuter, a murder, a defense-intelligence past. Baldacci’s recent thriller, standing at the right of the row.
books.whyItFits: The contemporary end of the paperback wall. Still a Halifax weekend book.

books.title: The Bourne Betrayal
books.author: Eric Van Lustbader (Robert Ludlum)
books.summary: Lustbader continuing Ludlum’s amnesiac assassin. Identity as a plot device and a job hazard.
books.whyItFits: Spy fiction as a run, not a one-off. The Ludlum franchise earns its slot next to Baldacci.

books.title: An Astronaut's Guide to Life on Earth
books.author: Chris Hadfield
books.summary: Hadfield on checklists, sweating the small stuff, and how to live somewhere hostile. Cover-up on the left stack — a Canadian copy in a Canadian house.
books.whyItFits: Competence as a personality. Hadfield is the civilian version of Extreme Ownership, with better photos of Earth.

books.title: Call Sign Chaos
books.author: Jim Mattis & Bing West
books.summary: Mattis on reading, command, and the three-boxes theory of a career. Under Hadfield on the left stack.
books.whyItFits: A general’s memoir under an astronaut’s. The collection’s competence stack is literal.

books.title: Barbarians at the Gate
books.author: Bryan Burrough & John Helyar
books.summary: RJR Nabisco, the LBO, and the most readable deal book ever written. Red spine at the bottom of the left stack.
books.whyItFits: King of Capital’s ancestor. Private equity as farce, which is how you actually learn it.

books.title: No Hero
books.author: Mark Owen with Kevin Maurer
books.summary: The sequel to No Easy Day: more SEAL work, less movie poster. Lying on the right stack as the current top of that pile.
books.whyItFits: Willink on the leadership bay; Owen on the stack. Same community, different register.

books.title: Unicorn in the Woods
books.author: Gordon Pitts
books.summary: Goose Lane: how an East Coast lab became a world-beating tech shop. Radian6, Salesforce, and the Atlantic Canada chip on the shoulder.
books.whyItFits: Halifax tech is not a footnote. Pitts wrote the local unicorn book and it belongs on this wall.

books.title: The End of the Free Market
books.author: Ian Bremmer
books.summary: Bremmer on state capitalism: when governments run the companies, and what that does to the old Washington-consensus story.
books.whyItFits: Dalio’s world-order book in plainer clothes. The stack is allowed to be about the system, not just the deal.

books.title: Devil Take the Hindmost
books.author: Edward Chancellor
books.summary: A history of financial speculation: tulips to tech, with the moral in the title. Under Bremmer on the right stack.
books.whyItFits: The Citco years in historical form. Chancellor is what ‘this time is different’ looks like the last twelve times.
